</font>

<td width="100%">
<font size=3 color="#ffffff" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman"><b>

Introduction
<font size=1><br><img src="line_grey.png"><br><br></font></b></font></td></tr></table>
</center>
<center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=2 color="#FFE291" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman">

This time I want to cover several forms of scene traversal algorithms
used to walk through common data structures. For the purposes of this
column I will be assuming that the reader is familiar with BSPs and
the concept of a portal. Like the fine culling systems overlap with 
the sorting properties of some of these approaches, some of these 
will share content with the visibility algorithms in the next 
installment of this column. <br><br>These algorithms generally require some form of visibility algorithm 
to be viable for a large scale scene. Some of these provide more 
information to a visibility algorithm than others; Some provide 
front-to-back ordering; Some work well in hardware environments;
Some work better in software; Some inherently provide their own 
visibility information through the traversal.<br><br>Next time I will be covering visibility algorithms that work in 
conjunction with these traversals and the fine culling algorithms from
the first column. Like the first one, this column is not meant to stand
on its own. <br><br>Note, in the traversals below I have not incorporated the logic to fit the
walk to the viewing frustum or to make the traversal obey an 
occlusion algorithm at all. This will be the subject of the next column.<br><br>This column is primarily intended to enumerate viable alternatives for use
in engines for realtime 3d gaming that have worked in my experience. 
I am not attempting to cover every algorithm extant. I leave that 
enterprise to some ambitious grad student needing a subject for a dissertation.
By no means do I wish to convey the misconception that this column can cover
everything of use in 3d graphics. My goal is to point out observations 
and comparisons between various algorithms and provide alternate methods 
to a developer stuck in a rut using a given approach.<br><br>Scene Traversals:
<blockquote>
<ul>
<b><li><a href="#bsptrees">BSP Trees</a></b>
<ul>
<li><a href="#bspfrontback">Planar Front-to-Back</a>
<li><a href="#bspfrontbackleafy">Leafy Front-to-Back</a><br><br><li><a href="#bspquake">Quake BSP/PVS</a>
</ul>
<b><li><a href="#portals">Portals</a></b>
<ul>
<li><a href="#portalsrecursive">Recursive Front-to-Back Traversal</a>
<li><a href="#portalskeyed">Keyed Queuing</a>
<li><a href="#portalspvs">Concave/PVS</a>
</ul>
<b><li><a href="#octrees">Octrees</a></b>
<ul>
<li><a href="#octh">Hierarchical Front-to-Back Traversal</a><br><br><li><a href="#octn">Neighbor Front-to-Back Traversal</a>
</ul>
<b><li><a href="#kdtrees">KD-Tree</a></b>
<ul>
<li><a href="#kdh">Hierarchical Front-to-Back Traversal</a>
<li><a href="#kdn">Neighbor Front-to-Back Traversal</a>
</ul>
<b><li><a href="#otheralgorithms">Other Structures</a></b><br>
<ul>
<li><a href="#feudal">Feudal Priority Trees</a><br>
<li><a href="#adaptive">Adaptive Octrees</a><br>
</ul>
<b><li><a href="issue02.htm#summary">Summary</a></b><br>
</ul>
</blockquote>
</font></td></tr></table>
</center><br><br><center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=3 color="#ffffff" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman"><b>

BSP Trees
<font size=1><br><img src="line_grey.png"><br><br></font></b></font></td></tr></table>
</center>
<center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=2 color="#FFE291" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman">

<a name="bsptrees">A BSP tree is quite frankly one of the most useful data structures 
    out there for 3d graphics.  Walking a BSP tree front-to-back is 
    virtually identical to a conventional binary tree's inorder traversal 
    The only difference is the definition of which of the children is the 
    first node to be visited depends upon the sign of the dot product of 
    the viewpoint and the plane normal of the parent node. I will refer 
    to three of the more useful forms of polygon storage in a BSP tree below.<br><br><!--Begin Front-Back Planar-->
<a name="bspfrontback">
<font size=2 face="Verdana,Helvetica" color="#ffff99"><i><u>Planar Front-to-Back:</i></u></font><br><br><blockquote>
      A Planar BSP is what people usually think about when someone mentions a
      BSP tree. In a planar tree, you can effectively ignore the leaves for
      rendering purposes. You start with all of your polygons in one bucket, 
      choose one via some heuristic, take that polygon and all polygons that
      a coplanar to it, create a BSP node, split the rest into two buckets and
      repeat until you have no polygon lying free in any bucket. Traversal of 
      a Planar BSP from front-to-back is basically a variant on a standard 
      binary tree inorder traversal. <br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">
      <font color="#0000ff">void</font> PlanarBSPNode::planar_ftb(<font color="#0000ff">const</font> Point & point) {
           <font color="#0000ff">int</font>   near = (point dot node.plane_normal >= 0.0);<br><br>           <font color="#0000ff">if</font> (child[near]) child[near]->planar_ftb(point);<br><br>           <font color="#0000ff">for</font> each polygon facing the near node in <font color="#0000ff">this</font> plane {
               polygon->render()
           }<br><br>           <font color="#0000ff">if</font> (child[near^1]) child[near^1]->planar_ftb(point);
      }
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>      Note: The 'render' routine for translucent polygons or polygons with
      transparencies places the polygons on a stack, which is popped away and
      rendered at the end of the frame.
</blockquote>
<!--End Front-Back Planar-->
<!--Begin Front-Back Leafy-->
<a name="bspfrontbackleafy">
<font size=2 face="Verdana,Helvetica" color="#ffff99"><i><u>Leafy Front-to-Back:</i></u></font><br><br><blockquote>
      A Leafy BSP is a useful data structure, often used by portal advocates as
      a quick-and-dirty means to obtain a portal set for arbitrary geometry.
      In addition to splitting as you walk down the BSP tree you then need to 
      walk back up the BSP tree splitting the contents of the parent planes as 
      you go. Afterwards you can organize the clipped polygon fragments into their 
      assorted leaves. When this is done you no longer track which polygons lie in a
      given plane of the BSP tree, but instead you track which polygons act 
      as faces for the individual BSP nodes.<br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">
      <font color="#0000ff">class</font> LeafyBSPCommonParent { 
           <font color="#007f00">// you can do this with typecasting and structs if need be.
</font>           ....
           <font color="#0000ff">void</font> leafy_ftb(<font color="#0000ff">const</font> Point & point); 
      }<br><br>      <font color="#0000ff">void</font> LeafyBSPNode::leafy_ftb(<font color="#0000ff">const</font> Point & point) {
           <font color="#0000ff">int</font>   near = (point dot node.plane_normal >= 0.0);
           child[near]->leafy_ftb(point);
           child[near^1]->leafy_ftb(point);
      }<br><br>      <font color="#0000ff">void</font> LeafyBSPLeaf::leafy_ftb(<font color="#0000ff">const</font> Point & point) {
           <font color="#0000ff">for</font> each polygon that forms a face that faces into <font color="#0000ff">this</font> node {
               polygon->render();
           }
      }
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center>
</blockquote>
<!--End Front-Back Leafy-->
<!--Begin Quake Bsp-->
<a name="bspquake">
<font size=2 face="Verdana,Helvetica" color="#ffff99"><i><u>Quake BSP:</i></u></font><br><br><blockquote>
      If you are using a front-end rasterization routine like passing directly to
      hardware, an S-Buffer, Active Edge List, or Active Edge Heap, then there is  
      little purpose to splitting the polygons as you walk down the BSP tree. Simply
      make a second reference to it in the compiler and all is well. If you allow 
      multiple references to a given polygon to float around the tree you can simply 
      adjust the polygon rendering routine to keep a frame index counter like the 
      following:<br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">
      <font color="#0000ff">void</font> Polygon::render() {
           <font color="#0000ff">if</font> (last_seen != frame_no) {
              last_seen = frame_no;
              ...do rendering here...
           }
      }
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>      The walk does not provide front-to-back ordering of the polygons. However in
      many cases you do not need this. It may cause additional overhead when dealing
      with translucent polygons (which will need to be sorted back to front).  Since 
      this walk will not provide front-to-back ordering in any event, there is little 
      point in doing the scene traversal inorder. Quake gets away with much this same 
      approach, by just taking the nodes from the potentially visible set and throwing 
      their contents down the pipeline at the Active Edge List or openGL hardware. <br><br>      In this case, the purpose of the BSP then is to provide convex subregions
      and to serve as an aid to collision detection. It does not serve any ordering
      function for visitation. 
</blockquote>
<!--End Quake Bsp-->
</font></td></tr></table>
</center><br><br><center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=3 color="#ffffff" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman"><b>

Portals
<font size=1><br><img src="line_grey.png"><br><br></font></b></font></td></tr></table>
</center>
<center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=2 color="#FFE291" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman">

<a name="portals">Before I cover the strengths and weaknesses of given portal traversals, I want to 
   cover the distinction between convex and concave node based portal engines. <br><br>      <font size=2 face="Verdana,Helvetica" color="#ffff99">Convex Node:</font><br>
      <blockquote>   
      A convex node engine only allows a convex polyhedron to act as a node. Portals 
      serve to connect individual nodes. Within a convex node engine it is quite possible 
      to get perfect front-to-back ordering. 
      </blockquote> 
      <font size=2 face="Verdana,Helvetica" color="#ffff99">Concave Node:</font><br>
      <blockquote> 
      A concave node engine allows just about anything to serve as a node. It could be a 
      room with some complex geometry, a BSP tree, an undulating mass of procedurally 
      generating flesh, etc... A concave node engine does not lend itself to easily
      providing front-to-back ordering. As such it is really only suitable to frontend 
      rasterizers such as hardware, S-Buffers, Active Edge Lists and Active Edge Heaps,
      like the Quake BSP approach above.
      </blockquote> 
   With this distinction in mind. I will proceed to the traversals generally used to 
   walk through a conventional portalized scene.<br><br><!--Begin Recursive-->
<a name="portalsrecursive">
<font size=2 face="Verdana,Helvetica" color="#ffff99"><i><u>Recursive Traversal:</i></u></font><br><br><blockquote>
      The most obvious portal traversal is recursive. The algorithm is generally 
      implemented something like the following:<br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">
      <font color="#0000ff">void</font> Node::visit(PortalSilhouette & silhouette) {
        <font color="#0000ff">if</font> (last_seen != this_frame) {
          last_seen = this_frame;
          <font color="#0000ff">for</font> each polygon <font color="#0000ff">do</font> {
            <font color="#0000ff">if</font> (s->is_a_portal) {
              Silhouette s = clip polygon <font color="#0000ff">using</font> silhouette planes
              next <font color="#0000ff">if</font> s is empty.
              s->remote_node->visit(s);
            } <font color="#0000ff">else</font> { 
              Polygon p = clipped polygon <font color="#0000ff">using</font> silhouette planes
              p->render();
            }
          }
        }
      }
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>      I cannot emphasize enough how poorly this algorithm scales up to higher polygon 
      counts. You may wind up visiting a node several times because you reach it through
      different nodes, and because of the recursive clipping you may have to render each
      polygon in multiple discrete fragments. This engine is usually built because it
      seems to show promise when your engine is just a few rooms. This algorithm is
      designed to work with convex nodes.
</blockquote>
<!--End Recursive-->
<!--Begin Keyed Queuing-->
<a name="portalskeyed">
<font size=2 face="Verdana,Helvetica" color="#ffff99"><i><u>Keyed Queuing:</i></u></font><br><br><blockquote>
       In an effort to fix the problems with the previous algorihm, another common variant
       that works if the nodes are obtained from a BSP tree is to use the BSP key for a given 
       node and viewpoint to provide a sorting criteria. This assumes that the data structure 
       used is roughly similar to that for the Leafy BSP above with the addition of portal 
       information for the empty faces shared with neighboring nodes. The concept of sorting 
       by a BSP key is introduced in Michael Abrash's Black Book.<br><br>       This walk involves a small binomial heap (priority queue) or sorted list of nodes not
       yet visited but adjacent to ones visited and visible. The contents of the queue are
       pulled off in front-to-back order, the nodes are rendered and checked for visible 
       neighbors, which are then placed on the priority queue sorted by their BSP key.<br><br>       There are two forms of BSP keys that I have used. One can be generated by walking the 
       BSP tree inorder from a given viewpoint while incrementing a counter at each leaf. The 
       other can be created by walking down the BSP tree towards a given node and by recording
       as a bitstring every place where the side of the plane the eye resides on differs
       from the side the given node lies on. Two of these bitstrings can be compared to 
       determine if a given node is nearer to the viewer than the other. <br><br>       Note even though this uses a BSP tree for sorting it is technically a portal algorithm
       because it traverses into its neighbors through the portals. The advantages this holds
       over Recursive Traversal is that a given node is only rendered once. The disadvantage
       is the cost of computing the keys.
</blockquote>
<!--End Keyed Queuing-->
<!--Begin Concave/PVS-->
<a name="portalspvs">
<font size=2 face="Verdana,Helvetica" color="#ffff99"><i><u>Concave/PVS:</i></u></font><br><br><blockquote>
       The simplest algorithm here for traversal is to allow anything to be in a node and to 
       maintain a potentially visible set between concave nodes. The traversal is identical to
       the Quake BSP traversal above. Collision can be much harder to detect and handle;
       Collision detection is very important in a game, so consider this solution with care.
       Other issues include detecting what node you are presently in in the absence of convex
       boundaries. Usual fixes include declaring the node to be convex in shape but containing
       arbitrary geometry. This is a nice fast-and-loose algorithm for getting polygons on the
       screen though.<br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">
       <font color="#0000ff">for</font> each node in the PVS <font color="#0000ff">for</font> the viewpoint {
           node->render();
       }  
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>       One could also use convex nodes for this algorithm which would improve collision 
       detection and may offer other benefits to AI and software rendering, but this still 
       leave determining the current node as a potential problem, if you have no a priori
       knowledge of the container for a point.
</blockquote>
<!--End Concave/PVS-->
</font></td></tr></table>
</center><br><br><center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=3 color="#ffffff" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman"><b>

Octrees
<font size=1><br><img src="line_grey.png"><br><br></font></b></font></td></tr></table>
</center>
<center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=2 color="#FFE291" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman">

<a name="octrees">An octree is a very simple data structure which has recently received a bit more
       hype than it is worth on its own. There is a decent Introduction to Octrees 
       by Jaap Suter in the tutorial section here on flipCode, so I will not attempt to 
       review that material here. Instead I will build upon it.<br><br>       Octrees are very well suited to particular tasks such as finding objects in a 
       given area, or locating likely polygons to attempt collision with; They are not 
       necessarily any better suited to dealing with a static polygon soup than another 
       structure is. By itself an octree does not provide a means of front-to-back 
       traversal of the individual polygons within a leaf, however there are at least
       two workable front-to-back traversal for walking amongst the nodes themselves. <br><br>       Different uses of this structure provide different answers as to what is the 
       best polygon count to stop at when subdividing the octree and what should be 
       used as a maximum recursion depth. <br><br>       A common implementation would resemble the following:<br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">
       <font color="#0000ff">class</font> octree_common {
           <font color="#007f00">// note you don't need to store these, you can carry them down with you
</font>           <font color="#007f00">// as you walk the structure but its easier to demonstrate this way.
</font>           <font color="#0000ff">float</font> min_z, max_z, min_y, max_y, min_x, max_x;
           <font color="#0000ff">float</font> avg_x() { <font color="#0000ff">return</font> (min_x + max_x)/2; }
           <font color="#0000ff">float</font> avg_y() { <font color="#0000ff">return</font> (min_y + max_y)/2; }
           <font color="#0000ff">float</font> avg_z() { <font color="#0000ff">return</font> (min_z + max_z)/2; }
 
       };<br><br>       <font color="#0000ff">class</font> octree_node : <font color="#0000ff">public</font> octree_common {
           octree_common * child[8];
       };<br><br>       <font color="#0000ff">class</font> octree_leaf : <font color="#0000ff">public</font> octree_common {
           polygon_list polygons;
           object_list  objects;
           ...
       };
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>       Ordering the contents of the octree leaves with miniature BSP trees may be useful
       if perfect front-to-back ordering of the polygons is desired for another purpose.<br><br><!--Begin Hierarchical Front-to-Back Traversal-->
<a name="octh">
<font size=2 face="Verdana,Helvetica" color="#ffff99"><i><u>Hierarchical Front-to-Back Traversal:</i></u></font><br><br><blockquote>Hierarchical traversal of an octree is based on the same plane separation principle 
       that makes a BSP front-to-back walk work. In this case, think of a single node with
       its eight children as mimicking 3 levels of a BSP tree:<br><br>
<center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">
                            z plane
                           /       \
                    y plane         y plane
                   /       \       /       \
              x plane  x plane  x plane  x plane
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>       All of the BSP traversals above will then work on the octree just as well as they 
       will on a BSP tree itself. However, observation can simplify some of these traversals.
       Given which side of the 3 planes subdividing an octree node that the eye point is on
       you can perform a simpler traversal based on bit toggling. You have three planes
       and thus 3 sign bits. If you toggle any one bit you will get one of the 3 nodes which
       share a face with the leaf in question. If you toggle all 3 bits you will get the 
       node in the far corner of the octree. Given this you can simply walk a given octree 
       node from front-to-back by the following sequence.<br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">
       octree_node::hierarchical_ftb(Point & eye) {
           <font color="#0000ff">int</font> first      = ((eye.x() &lt; avg_x()) ? 1 : 0) |
                            ((eye.y() &lt; avg_y()) ? 2 : 0) |
                            ((eye.z() &lt; avg_z()) ? 4 : 0);<br><br>           child[first].hierarchical_ftb(eye);<br><br>           child[first^1].hierarchical_ftb(eye); <font color="#007f00">// toggle bit 0 \ 
</font>           child[first^2].hierarchical_ftb(eye); <font color="#007f00">// toggle bit 1  these 3 can be in any order
</font>           child[first^4].hierarchical_ftb(eye); <font color="#007f00">// toggle bit 2 / 
</font>
           child[first^3].hierarchical_ftb(eye); <font color="#007f00">// toggle bits 0 & 1 \
</font>           child[first^5].hierarchical_ftb(eye); <font color="#007f00">// toggle bits 0 & 2  these 3 can be in any order
</font>           child[first^6].hierarchical_ftb(eye); <font color="#007f00">// toggle bits 1 & 2 / 
</font>
           child[first^7].hierarchical_ftb(eye); <font color="#007f00">// toggle bits 0, 1 & 2
</font>       }
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>       This walk has the benefit of simplicity. On the other hand it incurs the overhead of 
       walking through the hierarchy for the traversal. 
</blockquote>
<!--End Hierarchical Front-to-Back Traversal-->
<!--Begin Neighbor Front-to-Back Traversal-->
<a name="octn">
<font size=2 face="Verdana,Helvetica" color="#ffff99"><i><u>Neighbor Front-to-Back Traversal:</i></u></font><br><br><blockquote>
Neighbor Traversal requires some minor slight addition to the octree definition:<br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">
       <font color="#0000ff">class</font> octree_common {
             ...
             <font color="#0000ff">int</font> last_seen;
             ...
       }<br><br>       <font color="#0000ff">class</font> octree_leaf : <font color="#0000ff">public</font> octree_common {
             ...
             octree_common * neighbors[6];
             ...
       }  
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>       These six pointers represent the node that lies adjacent to this leaf through any
       of its six faces. <br><br>       If you are deeper or of equal depth in the tree than the neighbor is then one or 
       many little nodes will point into the same same-sized or larger adjacent node 
       through a common face. If you are at the same height as the neighboring node you 
       will both share the common face on a 1:1 correspondance. <br><br>       If you are higher in the tree then your one face will abutt have many leaves_
       on the one side of you. This is perfectly acceptable, and in this case you will 
       not attach to the leaf, but to the parent or grandparent node that is at the same 
       height as you in the tree. This is why the links are of an octree_common type 
       xrather than an octree_leaf. <br><br>       To traverse from front-to-back through this kind of scene is virtually identical
       to the Keyed Queuing approach mentioned in the Portal section above. The primary
       change required is when you link from a leaf to a parent node through a common
       face, you need to recursively walk down checking the 4 children that share that
       face's corresponding face for visibility.<br><br>       There are some consequences to the modifications that this requires to the 
       data structure. First of all, the neighbor links can become quite onerous to 
       maintain if your octree is rapidly changing. Secondly, your traversal is now
       complicated by a priority queue and other data structures which may complicate
       development.
</blockquote>
<!--End Neighbor Front-to-Back Traversal-->
</font></td></tr></table>
</center><br><br><center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=3 color="#ffffff" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman"><b>

KD-Trees
<font size=1><br><img src="line_grey.png"><br><br></font></b></font></td></tr></table>
</center>
<center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=2 color="#FFE291" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman">

<a name="kdtrees">A KD-Tree is nearly identical to a BSP tree.  The differences between a BSP and a 
       KD-tree include that a KD-Tree is forced to use axis aligned planes and the current 
       level of the tree is used to determine which axis to split along.<br><br>       A kd-tree node subdivides space into 2 smaller spaces like a BSP node. The additional
       restrictions upon a kd-tree are that the planes be axis aligned and the choice of 
       axis is based on the current level in the tree.<br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">
                            z plane
                           /       \
                    y plane         y plane
                   /       \       /       \
              x plane  x plane  x plane  x plane
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>       This is a classic kd-tree, and there exist many papers on the subject, off the 
       top of my head Seth Teller uses kd-trees in his paper on visibility determination 
       in densely occluded environments.<br><br>       Note that a kd-tree splits on one plane at a time. This allows it to fit better 
       than an octree, because the planes in the children can be at different offsets and
       because they fit to the data, allowing a relatively balanced structure.<br><br>       One modification to the 'classic' kd-tree structure is to allow the choice of plane 
       to split upon to vary at each level, this drives up your preprocessing cost by about 
       a factor of 3, and adds a small bit of data to the tree, but can theoretically 
       produce fewer splits, because you can choose your partitioning plane, by which 
       plane when it would divide the child sets into two equal buckets would produce 
       the fewest splits. Unfortunately this optimization, much like the balance vs. 
       split heuristics in BSP tree generation can lead to degenerately shaped kd-tree 
       nodes if left to run unchecked.<br><br><!--Begin Hierarchical Front-to-Back Traversal-->
<a name="kdh">
<font size=2 face="Verdana,Helvetica" color="#ffff99"><i><u>Hierarchical Front-to-Back Traversal:</i></u></font><br><br><blockquote>
       Hierarchical traversal of a kd-tree is identical to hierarchical traversal of an 
       octree as described above or to a front-to-back traversal of a BSP tree. 
</blockquote>
<!--End Hierarchical Front-to-Back Traversal-->
<!--Begin Neighbor Front-to-Back Traversal-->
<a name="kdn">
<font size=2 face="Verdana,Helvetica" color="#ffff99"><i><u>Neighbor Front-to-Back Traversal:</i></u></font><br><br><blockquote>
       Neighbor traversal of a kd-tree can be performed in a similar manner to the neighbor
       traversal of the octree above, but it is not as effective. The reason is because the 
       faces of the octree children at a given level all line up perfectly. In the kd-tree
       using the figure above, the two y aligned planes are likely to have chosen different
       offsets to split upon. This means that the neighbor traversal winds up severely 
       handicapped as the traversal algorithm has to walk down to the leaf from a higher 
       level node as the norm rather than the exception, unlike the octree neighbor traversal.
</blockquote>
<!--End Neighbor Front-to-Back Traversal-->
</font></td></tr></table>
</center><br><br><center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=3 color="#ffffff" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman"><b>

Other Algorithms
<font size=1><br><img src="line_grey.png"><br><br></font></b></font></td></tr></table>
</center>
<center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=2 color="#FFE291" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman">

<a name="otheralgorithms">
<a name="feudal">
<font size=2 face="Verdana,Helvetica" color="#ffff99"><i><u>Feudal Priority Trees:</i></u></font>
<blockquote>A feudal priority tree is a form of dynamic BSP tree suited to low polygon count
       environments. It has more relaxed requirements than a conventional BSP tree, but the
       runtime cost of using it can be much higher, and it doesn't scale well.<br><br>       <a target="_blank" href="http://www.scs.ryerson.ca/h2jang/archive-19980507.html">http://www.scs.ryerson.ca/h2jang/archive-19980507.html</a> contains a brief description
       and includes the names of several papers on the subject.
</blockquote>
<!--End Feudal Priority Trees-->
<!--Adaptive Octrees--><br><br><a name="adaptive">
<font size=2 face="Verdana,Helvetica" color="#ffff99"><i><u>Adaptive Octrees:</i></u></font><br><br><blockquote>
       An adaptive octree is an octree which allows the position of the split point in the 
       center of an octree node to be displaced. In practice, I tend to prefer a kd-tree 
       to an adaptive octree, but in some cases, the adaptive octree may consume less 
       memory. In addition, the neighbor front-to-back traversal of an adaptive octree 
       tends to be faster than for a kd-tree, because within a given octree node the 
       partitioning planes line up.
</blockquote>
<!--End Adaptive Octrees-->
</font></td></tr></table>
</center><br><br><center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=3 color="#ffffff" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman"><b>

Summary
<font size=1><br><img src="line_grey.png"><br><br></font></b></font></td></tr></table>
</center>
<center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=2 color="#FFE291" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman">

In summary, if you are writing a hardware only engine, a concave node based portal engine
   is probably a safe bet. The vagaries involved in collision in this environment can be 
   overcome. The only real difficulty is that given an arbitrary object in 3d space, it can 
   be a bit expensive to discover which nodes the object is touching, without tracking this
   information as the object moves around the level.<br><br>   Octrees and kd-trees serve as a spatial subdivision mechanism, in and of themselves they 
   cannot perform all polygon sorting, and in fact, on hardware you do not need polygon sorting
   except for surfaces with translucencies. <br><br>   Next time, I will be covering methods for visibility that combine structures from 
   both this and the previous issue.
<!-- End Summary --><br><br><i>Harmless</i><br>

explicit permission from the author (Edward Kmett).</font></i>
